title: Python preproc CPU investigation notes
content:
Purpose:
This doc captures our ad-hoc investigation into CPU-bound pre-processing on the serving path (what we've been calling "preproc"): request parse, input normalization, tokenization/encoding, and the threadpool glue that ties async network IO to the Python work. Goal: identify the dominant CPU hotspots, quantify their impact on tail latency and throughput, and propose low-risk mitigations we can roll out as A/B experiments.

Context / Why now:
- Increasing p99 latencies on hosted API during high-concurrency synthetic load (end of Jan 2026).
- Customer call flagged poor performance on small prompt workloads where model time is small; suspect CPU overhead dominates.
- Previous investigations focused on GPU-side kernels; this doc is CPU-centric.

Summary of findings (short):
- Pure Python parsing + tokenization path consumes ~40–60% of CPU cycles under mixed workloads.
- Request JSON parse + validation is ~10–15% of CPU; string allocations are a major part.
- Tokenization (pure Python UTF handling + regex cleanup) accounts for 25–35% of CPU in our current tokenizer shim.
- ThreadPoolExecutor handoffs and context switching cost ~5–8% and correlate with increased p99 when worker saturation occurs.
- Spawning extra worker threads (naively) helps throughput until GIL contention increases latency for short-running requests.

Environment / repro notes:
- Service: api-router (uvicorn + our Python adapter) on Intel c5a.4xlarge (8 vCPU) image used in dedicated simulation pool.
- Python: CPython 3.11.5 (default build, no special patching)
- Tokenizer: internal shim calling into a small C extension for vocab lookup in some paths, but heavy normalization in Python.
- Benchmark harness: local harness that sends concurrent HTTP/2 requests with uniform prompt length distribution.
- Tools used: py-spy (sampling), perf + flamegraph, cProfile (micro sampling), strace for syscalls, heapprof/tracemalloc for allocation hotspots.

Key commands used (repro locally):
- py-spy top (pid) --live --subprocesses --native
- perf record -F 99 -p <pid> --call-graph dwarf -o perf.data; perf script | stackcollapse-perf.pl | flamegraph.pl > perf.svg
- python -m cProfile -o cprof.out ./bench_client.py --concurrency 200

Representative profiling output (high level):
- py-spy (sampling):
  - 42% python::preproc.normalize_input
  - 28% python::preproc.tokenizer.encode_tokens
  - 12% python::router.handle_request (json loads + validation)
  - 6% threading::ThreadPoolExecutor._worker (context switch overhead)
  - rest: async/await scheduling + system call overhead

- cProfile snapshot (top 5 cumulative time):
  1. preproc.normalize_input - 5.4s
  2. tokenizer.encode_tokens - 3.8s
  3. json.loads - 1.2s
  4. _stream_write (async send) - 0.6s
  5. ThreadPoolExecutor._work - 0.4s

Microbenchmarks we ran:
- JSON parsing: compared builtin json.loads vs orjson (v5.10). orjson was ~3–4x faster on our small request blobs and reduced allocations. Replacing json.loads in router decreased router CPU by ~9% and p95 by ~6% in the synthetic harness.
- Tokenizer: isolated pure Python normalization (strip, regex replace, unicode_NFKC) vs compiled C extension + Rust tokenizer (local pyfasttokenizer shim). Results: Rust/C approach ~6–8x faster for normalization+split, and reduced Python heap churn substantially.
- Thread handoff: Experimented with two designs:
  - Async main loop -> ThreadPoolExecutor.submit(fn) for blocking work (current)
  - Dedicated worker pool (set of long-lived worker threads with bounded queue) and a non-blocking enqueue operation
  Observed: long-lived worker threads + bounded lock-free queue reduced enqueue latency and context switches by ~30%, but required safe shutdown logic.

Observed failure modes / tail cases:
- Heavy concurrency with many short prompts (1–10 tokens): per-request overhead dominates, so any small per-request allocation multiplies latency.
- Burstiness: sudden spikes cause threadpool queue growth; ThreadPoolExecutor creates new threads under load which causes CPU cycles for thread start + memory and increases p99 briefly.
- GIL saturation: when we offloaded more work into Python-level heavy loops (instead of C extensions), CPU utilization climbed and single-core latency spiked; throughput fell for small prompt workloads despite more workers.

Concrete numbers from one run (8 vCPU box, 500 rps steady, 200 concurrency):
- Baseline (current code): median RT 28ms, p95 130ms, p99 420ms, server CPU 78%
- Replace json.loads with orjson: median 24ms, p95 118ms, p99 380ms, server CPU 71%
- Replace tokenizer normalize with fast C/Rust shim: median 19ms, p95 95ms, p99 250ms, server CPU 54%
- Switch to bounded long-lived worker pool + C/Rust tokenizer: median 17ms, p95 88ms, p99 230ms, server CPU 52%

Hypotheses and root causes (ranked):
1) Python-level normalization (unicode handling, regex) is the dominant CPU consumer. Moving to a native implementation gives the largest win.
2) JSON parsing in pure Python has measurable cost — use orjson where safe. Validation/shape checks still run in Python and can be throttled or simplified.
3) ThreadPoolExecutor dynamic thread creation and handoffs cause latency spikes under burst; a bounded long-lived pool reduces variance.
4) GIL contention appears when many workers do Python-heavy work; mitigations: native tokenizer, or run CPU-heavy tasks in separate worker processes or native extensions.

Low-risk mitigations (fast experiments):
- Swap json.loads -> orjson in router path (feature flagged). Impact: small code change, immediate perf improvement.
- Introduce a flag to prefer bounded long-lived worker pool vs default ThreadPoolExecutor. Start in canary region.
- Instrument allocations and add tracemalloc hook to the preproc hot path to confirm object churn causes GC pauses.

Medium-impact mitigations (requires engineering work):
- Replace Python normalization code with a small Rust extension or call into existing Rust tokenizer (we have a pyfasttokenizer prototype). Prioritize the minimal API surface: normalize + split + offsets.
- Move request validation to a fast-path that skips deep checks when request size/shape matches a known template (add a robust guard).

Riskier / long-term changes:
- Run the entire preproc in a separate process pool (multiprocessing) to avoid GIL; adds IPC overhead and complexity for tracing/observability.
- Rework to a fully native server in Rust/Go for front-end preprocessing. Good long-term but large investment.

Observability suggestions (short):
- Add token-level cost attribution: emit per-request breakdown: parse_ms, normalize_ms, tokenize_ms, enqueue_ms, model_ms. Store these in traces.
- Add lightweight sampled flamegraphs (py-spy) in production for p99 queries to confirm behavior under customer workloads.
- Surface worker queue length and thread create/destroy events to console dashboard.

Action plan (next steps):
- Week 0: orjson swap behind feature flag + canary rollout (owner: Tom)
- Week 1: Add bounded long-lived worker pool implementation + load test (owner: Marta)
- Week 2: Integrate Rust native normalizer into preproc and run A/B against canary (owner: Aisha + Diego)
- Week 3: Evaluate multiprocessing worker model in a spike branch (owner: Diego)
- Ongoing: Add telemetry per-request for preproc stages; correlate with tail latency alerts (owner: eng-observability)

Open questions / TODOs:
- For orjson: are there edge-cases in our older clients with non-UTF8 that break? Need integration tests.
- Memory/regression risk of Rust tokenizer: verify memory safety and measure peak RSS under stress.
- How to safely do zero-downtime swap for worker pool changes across many replicas?

Notes from quick experiments (raw lines):
- py-spy sample:
  sample 1000 frames, 0.1s interval
  top 10: preproc.normalize_input (420)
           preproc.tokenizer.encode_tokens (280)
           json.loads (120)

- perf flame: heavy C stacks show memcpy called a lot during decode; heap churn visible in __libc_malloc.

Appendix: inexpensive test harness for local dev (script sketch):
- bench_preproc.py: spawn X worker threads and submit N raw request blobs, measure per-stage ms via time.perf_counter and print aggregate percentiles. Use randomized whitespace + unicode to mimic customer inputs.

Final thought:
We can get ~2x improvement for short prompt workflows by focusing on two changes: faster tokenizer (native) and faster JSON parsing. These are incremental and relatively low risk. Threadpool tuning produces additional variance reduction. Prioritize orjson swap + native normalizer prototype in canary; observe p99 change and allocation profiles before wider rollout.
